questions.title: Build and Display a Singly Linked List
questions.module: Module 17: Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues
questions.objective: Create linked nodes and append each new node at the tail.
questions.problem_statement:
Read N integers and insert them at the end of a singly linked list in input order. Print the list from head to tail. Implement your own nodes; do not store the values in an array or collection.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

Explanation: Each new node is linked after the current tail, so the list preserves the original input order.
questions.input_format: N, followed by N integers.
questions.output_format: Print the values separated by single spaces. If N = 0, print an empty line.
hints: A Node class holds an int value and a reference to the next node.
Keep a tail reference so each append takes O(1) time instead of walking the whole list.
A dummy head node avoids a special case for the first insertion.

questions.title: Reverse a Singly Linked List
questions.module: Module 17: Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues
questions.objective: Reverse a linked list in place by redirecting each node's next pointer.
questions.problem_statement:
Reverse the links of a singly linked list in place. The original last node becomes the head. Do not create replacement data nodes or use an array to store the values.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

Explanation: Each node's next pointer is redirected to its previous node, reversing the traversal order.
questions.input_format: N, followed by N integers.
questions.output_format: Print the reversed list on one line. If N = 0, print an empty line.
hints: Walk the list with three references: prev, cur, and next.
Save cur.next before overwriting it with prev, or the rest of the list is lost.
When cur becomes null, prev is the new head.

questions.title: Find the Middle Node
questions.module: Module 17: Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues
questions.objective: Locate the middle of a list in one pass with slow and fast pointers.
questions.problem_statement:
Find the middle node of a singly linked list. For an even number of nodes, return the second middle node. Use slow and fast pointers without counting the nodes in a separate traversal.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

Explanation: The slow pointer advances one node for every two nodes traversed by the fast pointer. When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is at the second middle node.
questions.input_format: N, followed by N integers.
questions.output_format: Print the middle value. If the list is empty, print EMPTY.
hints: Start both pointers at the head.
Loop while fast != null && fast.next != null, moving slow one step and fast two steps.
With this loop condition, an even-length list stops at the second middle node.

extra_fields.input_format: N, followed by N integers.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the middle value. If the list is empty, print EMPTY.

questions.title: Implement a Stack Using a Linked List
questions.module: Module 17: Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues
questions.objective: Implement push and pop at the head of a linked list in O(1) time.
questions.problem_statement:
Implement a stack using your own singly linked nodes. Support PUSH x, POP, PEEK, and SIZE. PUSH adds an element to the top; POP removes and prints the top; PEEK prints the top without removing it; SIZE prints the current size. POP and PEEK on an empty stack print EMPTY. Each stack operation must take O(1) time, excluding output costs.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

Explanation: The stack is last-in, first-out (LIFO). The first POP removes 20, leaving only 10; the final POP finds the stack empty.
questions.input_format: Q, followed by Q commands.
questions.output_format: Print a result for each POP, PEEK, or SIZE command. PUSH produces no output.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ Q ≤ 100,000
Pushed values fit in int.
sample_inputs:
7
PUSH 10
PUSH 20
PEEK
POP
SIZE
POP
POP
hints: The top of the stack is the head of the list: push creates a node pointing to the old head.
Keep a size counter instead of counting nodes for every SIZE command.
Collect output in a StringBuilder and print once; 200,000 separate println calls can be slow.

questions.title: Check Balanced Brackets
questions.module: Module 17: Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues
questions.objective: Match nested brackets with a stack.
questions.problem_statement:
Given a string containing only (, ), [, ], {, and }, determine whether the brackets are balanced. Each closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opening bracket. Use a stack.

hints: Push every opening bracket.

After the scan, the stack must be empty: a leftover opening bracket also means NO.

Remove the Nth node from the end of a singly linked list. N is guaranteed to be between 1 and the list length. Use two pointers so the node can be located without first calculating the list length in a separate traversal.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

Move the fast pointer N steps ahead first, then move both pointers until fast reaches the last node.

questions.title: Detect a Cycle in a Linked List
questions.module: Module 17: Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues
questions.objective: Detect a cycle with Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm using O(1) extra space.
questions.problem_statement:
A linked list has N nodes numbered from 0 to N − 1. Each node has a value and a next-node index. A next index of -1 means no next node. The head is node 0 when N is positive.

Determine whether following links from the head eventually revisits a node. Use Floyd's slow-and-fast pointer technique or another method with O(1) auxiliary space. A cycle that cannot be reached from node 0 does not count.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

Explanation: Following node 0 leads to 1, then 2, then 3, and then back to 1. The traversal therefore repeats nodes indefinitely.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N. Each of the next N lines contains a node value and its next-node index.
questions.output_format: Print CYCLE if a cycle is reachable from the head; otherwise, print NO CYCLE.
questions.constraints:
0 ≤ N ≤ 200,000
Each next index is −1 or between 0 and N − 1.
hints: Create the N nodes first, then set each node's next reference from its index.
Move slow one step and fast two steps; if they ever meet, there is a cycle.
If fast reaches null, the list ends and there is no cycle. An empty list has no cycle.

hints: Use a dummy head and a tail pointer for the merged list.
Attach whichever current node is smaller, then advance in that list.
When one list runs out, attach the rest of the other list in a single step.

questions.title: Evaluate a Postfix Expression
questions.module: Module 17: Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues
questions.objective: Evaluate postfix notation with a stack of operands.
questions.problem_statement:
Evaluate a valid postfix expression containing integer operands and the binary operators +, -, *, and /. Tokens are separated by spaces. Use a stack: when an operator is encountered, pop the right operand first, then the left operand. Division truncates toward zero. Division by zero does not occur, and all intermediate results fit in a long.

Input hint: A token is the subtraction operator only when it is exactly -. A token such as -3 is a negative number.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

Explanation: First calculate 3 × 4 = 12. Then calculate 12 + 12 = 24, and finally 24 − 2 = 22.
questions.input_format: One line containing the postfix expression.
questions.output_format: Print the final integer result.
hints: Read the line and split it on whitespace: line.trim().split("\\s+").
Push numbers as long values. For an operator, pop b (the right operand) and then a, and push a op b.
Java's long division already truncates toward zero, so -7 / 2 is -3.

For each array element, find the first element to its right that is strictly greater. If no such element exists, return -1. Use a monotonic stack to solve the problem in O(N) time. Equal values are not greater.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

hints: Keep a stack of indices whose next greater element hasn't been found yet.
For each new value, pop every index whose value is strictly smaller and record the new value as its answer.
Indices still on the stack at the end have no greater element, so their answer is −1.

questions.title: Merge K Sorted Linked Lists
questions.module: Module 17: Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues
questions.objective: Merge K sorted lists with a min-priority queue of their current heads.
questions.problem_statement:
You are given K singly linked lists, each sorted in non-decreasing order. Merge all the lists into one sorted list. Reuse existing nodes instead of creating replacement data nodes for every value.

Use a min-priority queue containing the current smallest available node from each non-empty list. The required time complexity is O(T log K) when K is greater than 1, where T is the total number of nodes.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

Explanation: The priority queue repeatedly supplies the smallest available node among the list heads. After a node is appended, the next node from that same list becomes a candidate.
questions.input_format:
The first line contains K.
Each of the next K lines begins with the length of that list, followed by its values in sorted order.
An empty list is represented by 0.
questions.output_format: Print the merged list on one line, with values separated by single spaces. If all lists are empty or K = 0, print an empty line.
questions.constraints:
0 ≤ K ≤ 100,000
Total number of nodes T ≤ 200,000
Values fit in int.
hints: Build each list from its line, then add every non-null head to a PriorityQueue<Node> ordered by Integer.compare(a.val, b.val).
Poll the smallest node, append it to the result, and offer its next node if there is one.
Compare with Integer.compare, not subtraction, because values span the full int range.

questions.objective: Combine a HashMap with your own doubly linked list for O(1) LRU operations.
questions.problem_statement:
Implement a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache with capacity C. Each entry stores an integer key and integer value. When the cache is full and a new key is inserted, evict the least recently used entry.

Support these commands:
- PUT key value: insert a new entry or update an existing entry. The key becomes the most recently used.
- GET key: print the value if the key exists; otherwise, print -1. A successful access makes the key most recently used.
Unlike a library-based LRU implementation such as an access-ordered LinkedHashMap, use java.util.HashMap only for key lookup and build the recency order with your own doubly linked list. GET and PUT must take O(1) average time. Updating an existing key must not create a duplicate entry or evict another key. If C = 0, ignore every PUT and return -1 for every GET.

Implementation requirement: Use the hash map for direct lookup and the doubly linked list to move entries to the most-recently-used position and remove the least-recently-used entry efficiently.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

Explanation: GET 1 makes key 1 most recently used. Inserting key 3 evicts key 2, the least recently used entry. Key 1 remains available, and key 3 can be retrieved.
questions.input_format: The first line contains C and Q. The next Q lines contain either PUT key value or GET key.
questions.output_format: Print one line for each GET command. PUT produces no output.
questions.constraints:
0 ≤ C ≤ 100,000
1 ≤ Q ≤ 200,000
Keys and values fit in int.
sample_inputs:
2 7
PUT 1 10
PUT 2 20
GET 1
PUT 3 30
GET 2
GET 3
GET 1
hints: Use sentinel head and tail nodes so insertions and removals never deal with null neighbors.
To mark a node as most recently used, unlink it and insert it right after the head.
When inserting a new key into a full cache, remove the node just before the tail and delete its key from the map.
